चीनले स्वदेशमै विकास गरेको १० मेट्रिक टन क्षमताको विद्युतीय व्यावसायिक विमान सीई-२५ए (CE-25A) ले पहिलोपटक चालकसहितको परीक्षण उडान सफलतापूर्वक पूरा गरेको छ। छोटो दूरीका व्यावसायिक हवाई यात्रामा विद्युतीय प्रविधि प्रयोग गर्ने चीनको प्रयासमा यसलाई महत्त्वपूर्ण उपलब्धिका रूपमा हेरिएको छ।

चीनको शान्दोङ प्रान्तस्थित बिन्झाउमा शनिबार गरिएको परीक्षण उडानमा दुई जना पाइलट र एक जना उडान परीक्षण इन्जिनियर सहभागी थिए। कुल ५७ मिनेट ४६ सेकेन्ड चलेको परीक्षणका क्रममा विमान १६ मिनेट ३८ सेकेन्ड आकाशमा रह्यो र ६०.४ किलोमिटर दूरी तय गर्‍यो।

विमान निर्माता चाइना कमर्सियल एयरक्राफ्ट कर्पोरेसन (कोम्याक) का अनुसार परीक्षणका क्रममा विमानको प्रदर्शन सामान्य रहेको र सबै नतिजा अपेक्षाअनुरूप आएका छन्।

सीई-२५ए चीनमा विकास गरिएको पहिलो विद्युतीय व्यावसायिक विमान हो। यसलाई दुई सहरबीचको छोटो दूरीको यात्राका लागि १९ जना यात्रु बोक्न सक्ने गरी डिजाइन गरिएको छ।

विमानको अधिकतम उडान भार १० मेट्रिक टन रहेको छ भने यसले प्रतिघण्टा ३०० किलोमिटरको क्रुज गति लिन सक्छ। त्यस्तै, यसको अधिकतम उडान उचाइ २ हजार ४०० मिटर र उडान दूरी ४०० किलोमिटर रहेको छ।

विमानका पखेटामा जडान गरिएका डिस्ट्रिब्युटेड इलेक्ट्रिक डक्टेड-फ्यान प्रणालीमार्फत यसलाई शक्ति प्रदान गरिन्छ। यस प्रविधिले विद्युतीय शक्तिको प्रयोगबाट विमान सञ्चालन गर्न सहयोग गर्छ।

चालकसहितको परीक्षण उडानअघि गत फेब्रुअरी २ मा सीई-२५ए को पहिलो मानवरहित स्वचालित परीक्षण उडान गरिएको थियो। कोम्याकका अनुसार विकास प्रक्रियाका क्रममा विमानले १९ पटक मानवरहित स्वचालित उडान परीक्षण पूरा गरिसकेको छ।

यो विमान कोम्याक, चिनियाँ ब्याट्री निर्माता कन्टेम्पोररी एम्पेरेक्स टेक्नोलोजी (सीएटीएल), साङ्घाई जियाओतोङ विश्वविद्यालयलगायत संस्थाको संयुक्त सहकार्यमा विकास भइरहेको हो।

यसैबीच, चीनको नागरिक उड्डयन प्रशासनले सीई-२५ए को टाइप सर्टिफिकेटका लागि परेको आवेदन स्वीकार गरेको छ। यसलाई विमानको प्रमाणीकरण प्रक्रियामा भएको महत्त्वपूर्ण प्रगतिका रूपमा हेरिएको छ।

सीई-२५ए लाई ठूला व्यावसायिक यात्रुवाहक विमानमा समेत लागू हुने चीनको सीसीएआर-२५ हवाईयोग्यता मापदण्डअनुसार विकास गरिएको छ। यद्यपि, व्यावसायिक उडान सुरु गर्नुअघि विमानले आवश्यक प्रमाणीकरण प्रक्रिया पूरा गर्नुपर्नेछ।

विद्युतीय प्रविधिमा आधारित यो विमानले भविष्यमा छोटो दूरीका हवाई यात्रालाई थप वातावरणमैत्री बनाउन सक्ने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ। तर यसको व्यावसायिक सञ्चालन सुरु हुन भने प्रमाणीकरण प्रक्रिया पूरा हुन आवश्यक छ।

Bodybuilder Eddie Abbew Calls Whey Protein a ‘Scam’: ‘Just Eat an Egg’
The former professional bodybuilder questions the supplement industry's marketing claims, citing personal digestive problems and advocating whole-food protein sources.

Former professional bodybuilder Eddie Abbew has criticised the widespread use of whey protein supplements, arguing that people should prioritise whole foods such as eggs to meet their daily protein requirements.

In a video titled The Real Reason Why I Stopped Drinking Whey Protein!, shared on YouTube, Abbew outlined five reasons behind his decision to stop consuming the popular bodybuilding supplement.

Known for his outspoken views on fitness and nutrition, Abbew questioned the supplement industry's influence on bodybuilding culture and challenged the idea that protein powders are essential for building muscle.

"If you want protein, eat a f***ing egg," he said in the video.
Five reasons behind his decision
Abbew explained that his first concern involved the origins and processing of whey protein. He claimed that whey was historically treated as a dairy by-product and that its transformation into a widely marketed fitness supplement was driven partly by commercial interests.

He also recalled how bodybuilding magazines and prominent athletes helped popularise whey protein during the 1990s, making it a staple among fitness enthusiasts.

His second and third concerns were related to his personal health experiences.

Abbew said he had experienced persistent testicular discomfort and digestive problems, including diarrhoea, while consuming whey protein. He recalled removing the supplement from his diet after receiving a social media comment questioning its possible effects on prostate health.

According to Abbew, his discomfort improved after he stopped consuming whey protein.

He also described experiencing frequent bloating after drinking protein shakes, which he partly associated with his lactose intolerance.

However, these are his personal experiences and do not independently establish that whey protein caused his symptoms.
Questions over ingredients and marketing
The fourth reason involved the ingredients used in commercial protein powders.

Abbew criticised products containing multiple additives, flavourings, thickeners and other processed ingredients. During the video, he read out the ingredient list of a whey protein product and argued that consumers should pay closer attention to what they are purchasing.

He described the product as more of a science experiment than food and questioned why people rely so heavily on processed supplements when protein is available through everyday foods.

His fifth concern focused on scientific research and the marketing of whey protein.

Abbew questioned whether some studies promoting whey protein were influenced by companies with commercial interests in the supplement industry. He also challenged claims about its bioavailability and absorption.

He argued that people should consider the broader nutritional value of their diets rather than focusing exclusively on protein intake.
Whole foods versus protein supplements
Throughout the video, Abbew encouraged viewers to obtain protein from whole-food sources, including eggs, meat, fish and chicken.

He argued that bodybuilding nutrition should not depend excessively on commercially marketed supplements.

However, whey protein is a dairy-derived protein that provides essential amino acids and can be a convenient way to increase protein intake. Its nutritional value and suitability depend on the individual, product formulation and dietary needs.

People with lactose intolerance may also experience digestive discomfort from certain whey products, although lactose-free alternatives are available.

Abbew's comments have brought renewed attention to the debate over protein supplements and the role of whole foods in bodybuilding.

While his personal experiences explain why he stopped consuming whey protein, his broader claims about its safety and nutritional value should not be treated as established scientific conclusions.

India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) has defended the government's authority over visa decisions, describing them as sovereign functions, following reports that Norwegian journalist Helle Lyng and several other foreign invitees faced visa denials or cancellations ahead of the Bharat Summit in Hyderabad.

Speaking at his regular media briefing on Friday, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said visa decisions fall within the sovereign authority of individual governments.

"Visa matters are sovereign functions of any country or any government. So that is what I have to say," Jaiswal stated.

His remarks came amid reports that more than 100 foreign invitees to the Bharat Summit had their visas denied or revoked, while over 300 others reportedly received clearance to attend the event.

Norwegian Journalist Says Visa Was Cancelled Before Departure
Helle Lyng, an independent journalist based in Norway, claimed that her Indian visa was cancelled shortly before she was due to leave for Hyderabad.

Lyng had been invited as a panelist and speaker at the Bharat Summit, where she was scheduled to participate in a discussion on the future of media and press freedom.

In a post on X, she questioned the decision, saying she had already received a visa from the Indian Embassy in Norway and was preparing to travel when it was revoked.

She alleged that the cancellation came on the instructions of higher authorities in India's Ministry of Home Affairs.

Lyng had previously attracted attention during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Oslo in May, when she raised a question concerning press freedom with the Indian side.

Congress Criticises Government Over Visa Cancellation
The Congress party strongly criticised the reported cancellation of Lyng's visa, questioning the government's response to journalists raising difficult questions.

In a post on X, the opposition party referred to Lyng's earlier interaction with Modi and questioned why she was prevented from attending the Hyderabad summit.

The party also raised concerns over the government's approach towards questions about press freedom and accountability.

Bharat Summit Held in Hyderabad
The Bharat Summit, organised by the Congress, is being held in Hyderabad on November 13 and 14.

Lyng was among the invited international participants expected to contribute to discussions on media, journalism and press freedom.

The reported visa cancellations have drawn attention to the participation of foreign speakers at the event, although the MEA has maintained that visa decisions remain within the sovereign authority of governments.

“HE SAW THE WIRE AND BOMB UNDER THE CLOAK: HE TACKLED HIM WITH HIS BARE HANDS.”

On August 8, 2012, in the crowded streets of Asadabad, Kunar Province, Afghanistan, a joint patrol of American commanders and provincial leaders was walking toward the provincial governor’s compound when an unthinkable threat emerged.

Serving as the personal security detachment commander for the 4th Infantry Division's 4th Brigade Combat Team, Captain Florent “Flo” Groberg was scanning the perimeter when he noticed an individual acting suspiciously on the left side of the street, walking backward toward the patrol formation.

As the man pivoted, Groberg spotted a suicide bomb vest concealed under the man’s cloak, complete with protruding trigger wires.

With less than two seconds to react, Captain Groberg made an instantaneous decision that saved dozens of lives:

Charging the Threat: Groberg yelled a warning, abandoned cover, and charged straight at the bomber, physically shoving him backward away from the command group.

Tackling Him to the Ground: Teaming up with Sergeant Andrew Mahoney, Groberg drove the bomber into the dirt, pinning the vest against the ground with his bare hands to absorb the blast.

Disrupting the Attack: The vest detonated against the earth. The downward blast blew Groberg 20 feet into a culvert, severing 50% of his calf muscle, shattering his fibula, and causing severe burns, but preventing the primary fragmentation wave from tearing through the command group.

Triggering the Second Bomber: The shockwave caused a second concealed suicide bomber nearby to detonate prematurely into an exterior wall before he could reach the patrol.

Four American heroes were killed in the ambush—Command Sgt. Maj. Kevin J. Griffin, Maj. Thomas E. Kennedy, Air Force Maj. Walter D. Gray, and foreign service officer Ragaei Abdelfattah—but dozens more survived because Captain Groberg physically threw his body onto the threat.

On November 12, 2015, President Barack Obama presented Captain Florent Groberg with the Medal of Honor at the White House.

“HE HAD A FRACTION OF A SECOND TO SAVE HIS MEN. HE CHOSE TO SACRIFICE HIMSELF.” — The Courage of Marine Corporal Jason Dunham.

On April 14, 2004, near the Syrian border in Husaybah, Iraq, 22-year-old Marine Corporal Jason Dunham was leading a rifle squad with 3rd Battalion, 7th Marines (3/7), moving to relieve a battalion commander’s convoy that had been ambushed.

After intercepting a line of suspicious vehicles attempting to flee the area, Dunham moved in on foot to conduct a search:

 As Dunham approached, an insurgent leaped from one of the vehicles and attacked him. Dunham immediately engaged the fighter in violent hand-to-hand combat to subdue him.

During the wrestling match on the dirt road, the insurgent pulled the pin on a hand grenade and dropped it between them.

Spotting two of his Marines—Lance Corporal William Hampton and PFC Kelly Miller—rushing in to assist him, Dunham shouted a warning: “No, no, watch out!” Without hesitation, he unstrapped his Kevlar helmet, slammed it over the grenade, and threw his entire body on top, pressing down with both hands to smother the blast.

The grenade exploded, shredding the helmet and mortally wounding Dunham. But his body and helmet absorbed the overwhelming force of the blast, saving both of his fellow Marines from fatal shrapnel.

Corporal Dunham was evacuated and succumbed to his wounds eight days later on April 22, 2004, at Bethesda Naval Hospital with his parents at his bedside.

On January 11, 2007, President George W. Bush presented the Medal of Honor posthumously to his family, making Jason Dunham the first Marine in the Iraq War to receive the nation’s highest military decoration. His legacy lives on across the fleet aboard the guided-missile destroyer USS Jason Dunham (DDG-109).

In an era where so few bear the burden of service, what does Corporal Jason Dunham’s split-second decision to smother a live grenade tell us about the heart of an American Marine?

“23 POUNDS OF STEEL. HUNDREDS OF ROUNDS OF 7.62. WELCOME TO THE JUNGLE.” — The Brutal Reality of Humping “The Pig” in Vietnam.

In the dense, suffocating heat of the Vietnamese jungle, infantrymen gave the M60 machine gun a nickname that stuck for generations: “The Pig.”

It earned the name honestly—because of its bulky, cumbersome weight, ferocious appetite for belted ammunition, and bone-jarring recoil when ripping through the brush:

• The Physical Punishment: At 23.15 pounds unloaded, the M60 was already a beast to carry. Factor in a spare barrel, an asbestos heat mitt, cleaning kit, and 500 to 1,000 rounds of linked 7.62×51mm NATO ammunition draped in crisscrossed bandoliers across the gunner and assistant gunner's chests, and a gun team was humping 70+ pounds through chest-high, razor-sharp elephant grass and knee-deep mud in 100-degree humidity.

• The Squad’s Lifeline: Firing at a sustained 550 to 650 rounds per minute with an effective range of over 1,100 meters, the M60 was the squad's primary base of fire. When an infantry patrol walked into an L-shaped ambush in the triple canopy, the distinctive heavy thumping roar of "The Pig" chewing through tree trunks was the only thing that bought troops time to maneuver.

• The Quirks: Early models lacked a carrying handle on the barrel, forcing gunners to use a bulky asbestos mitt to swap out glowing-red barrels mid-firefight. It was prone to jamming in red clay dust and mud, but when properly cleaned and fed, it delivered unmatched stopping power.

To the veterans who carried or fought alongside "The Pig" in Vietnam, the Gulf, or beyond: did you love it for its devastating firepower, or curse it every time you had to hump it up a ridgeline?

Fighting Traumatic Shock: He treated the victim for hypovolemic shock and kept her conscious until Fayetteville Police and EMS arrived, saving her life.

He refused to carry a weapon into battle. His own side called him a coward for it.

Desmond Doss was a Seventh-day Adventist who believed he could serve his country without taking a life. The Army mocked him and tried to push him out, then trained him as a combat medic and sent him to the Pacific.

On Okinawa, in the spring of 1945, his unit had to climb a cliff some 400 feet high that the men called Hacksaw Ridge. When a Japanese counterattack forced the Americans back, dozens of wounded were left stranded at the top. Doss refused to leave.

Alone and under fire, he went back again and again, lowering wounded men down the cliff face one at a time with a rope sling. Each time, he prayed the same thing: "Lord, please help me get one more." He kept going for hours. The Army credits him with saving about 75 men that day.

Days later he was wounded by a grenade, rolled off his own rescue litter to treat another man, and was then hit by a sniper. He splinted his shattered arm with a rifle stock and crawled to safety.

In 1945, he became the first conscientious objector in American history to receive the Medal of Honor. He never fired a shot at the enemy, and he saved more lives in one day than most men save in a lifetime.

On Sept. 8, 2009, during the Battle of Ganjgal in Kunar Province, Afghanistan, 21-year-old Marine Cpl. Dakota Meyer and Staff Sgt. Juan Rodriguez-Chavez heard their brothers trapped in a brutal ambush.

Denied permission four times to go in, Meyer defied orders, climbed into the gun turret of a Humvee, and charged into the kill zone five separate times across a six-hour firefight. Even after taking shrapnel to his arm, he helped rescue 36 Afghan and U.S. personnel and fought on foot to recover the bodies of his four fallen teammates — 1st Lt. Michael Johnson, Staff Sgt. Aaron Kenefick, Gunnery Sgt. Edwin Johnson, and Hospital Corpsman 3rd Class James Layton.

The Marines rejected him. So did the Navy and the paratroopers. He was too small and too young-looking, barely 5'5" and slight.

Three years later, Audie Murphy was the most decorated American soldier of World War II.

Born into a poor Texas sharecropping family, one of twelve children, he left school around the fifth grade to pick cotton. He finally got into the Army in 1942 and fought across Sicily, Italy, Anzio, France, and Germany with the 3rd Infantry Division.

On January 26, 1945, near Holtzwihr, France, his depleted company was attacked by German infantry and tanks. Murphy ordered his men back, then climbed onto a burning tank destroyer and used its machine gun to hold off the enemy almost single-handedly for nearly an hour, wounded, directing artillery by phone. For that, he earned the Medal of Honor.

He went on to Hollywood, made more than 40 films, and played himself in "To Hell and Back." He also spoke openly about the nightmares war left him, long before anyone called it PTSD.

He died in 1971 and rests at Arlington, his grave one of the most visited in America.

“I was off-duty, sitting in traffic in Nairobi having coffee, when the explosions and automatic gunfire echoed across the city.

“HE SAW THE WIRE AND BOMB UNDER THE CLOAK: HE TACKLED HIM WITH HIS BARE HANDS.”

On August 8, 2012, in the crowded streets of Asadabad, Kunar Province, Afghanistan, a joint patrol of American commanders and provincial leaders was walking toward the provincial governor’s compound when an unthinkable threat emerged.

Serving as the personal security detachment commander for the 4th Infantry Division's 4th Brigade Combat Team, Captain Florent “Flo” Groberg was scanning the perimeter when he noticed an individual acting suspiciously on the left side of the street, walking backward toward the patrol formation.

As the man pivoted, Groberg spotted a suicide bomb vest concealed under the man’s cloak, complete with protruding trigger wires.

With less than two seconds to react, Captain Groberg made an instantaneous decision that saved dozens of lives:

Charging the Threat: Groberg yelled a warning, abandoned cover, and charged straight at the bomber, physically shoving him backward away from the command group.

Tackling Him to the Ground: Teaming up with Sergeant Andrew Mahoney, Groberg drove the bomber into the dirt, pinning the vest against the ground with his bare hands to absorb the blast.

Disrupting the Attack: The vest detonated against the earth. The downward blast blew Groberg 20 feet into a culvert, severing 50% of his calf muscle, shattering his fibula, and causing severe burns, but preventing the primary fragmentation wave from tearing through the command group.

Triggering the Second Bomber: The shockwave caused a second concealed suicide bomber nearby to detonate prematurely into an exterior wall before he could reach the patrol.

Four American heroes were killed in the ambush—Command Sgt. Maj. Kevin J. Griffin, Maj. Thomas E. Kennedy, Air Force Maj. Walter D. Gray, and foreign service officer Ragaei Abdelfattah—but dozens more survived because Captain Groberg physically threw his body onto the threat.

On November 12, 2015, President Barack Obama presented Captain Florent Groberg with the Medal of Honor at the White House.

“Courage is not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it.”

“HE HAD A FRACTION OF A SECOND TO SAVE HIS MEN. HE CHOSE TO SACRIFICE HIMSELF.” — The Courage of Marine Corporal Jason Dunham.

On April 14, 2004, near the Syrian border in Husaybah, Iraq, 22-year-old Marine Corporal Jason Dunham was leading a rifle squad with 3rd Battalion, 7th Marines (3/7), moving to relieve a battalion commander’s convoy that had been ambushed.

After intercepting a line of suspicious vehicles attempting to flee the area, Dunham moved in on foot to conduct a search:

 As Dunham approached, an insurgent leaped from one of the vehicles and attacked him. Dunham immediately engaged the fighter in violent hand-to-hand combat to subdue him.

During the wrestling match on the dirt road, the insurgent pulled the pin on a hand grenade and dropped it between them.

Spotting two of his Marines—Lance Corporal William Hampton and PFC Kelly Miller—rushing in to assist him, Dunham shouted a warning: “No, no, watch out!” Without hesitation, he unstrapped his Kevlar helmet, slammed it over the grenade, and threw his entire body on top, pressing down with both hands to smother the blast.

The grenade exploded, shredding the helmet and mortally wounding Dunham. But his body and helmet absorbed the overwhelming force of the blast, saving both of his fellow Marines from fatal shrapnel.

Corporal Dunham was evacuated and succumbed to his wounds eight days later on April 22, 2004, at Bethesda Naval Hospital with his parents at his bedside.

On January 11, 2007, President George W. Bush presented the Medal of Honor posthumously to his family, making Jason Dunham the first Marine in the Iraq War to receive the nation’s highest military decoration. His legacy lives on across the fleet aboard the guided-missile destroyer USS Jason Dunham (DDG-109).

In an era where so few bear the burden of service, what does Corporal Jason Dunham’s split-second decision to smother a live grenade tell us about the heart of an American Marine?

“23 POUNDS OF STEEL. HUNDREDS OF ROUNDS OF 7.62. WELCOME TO THE JUNGLE.” — The Brutal Reality of Humping “The Pig” in Vietnam.

In the dense, suffocating heat of the Vietnamese jungle, infantrymen gave the M60 machine gun a nickname that stuck for generations: “The Pig.”

It earned the name honestly—because of its bulky, cumbersome weight, ferocious appetite for belted ammunition, and bone-jarring recoil when ripping through the brush:

• The Physical Punishment: At 23.15 pounds unloaded, the M60 was already a beast to carry. Factor in a spare barrel, an asbestos heat mitt, cleaning kit, and 500 to 1,000 rounds of linked 7.62×51mm NATO ammunition draped in crisscrossed bandoliers across the gunner and assistant gunner's chests, and a gun team was humping 70+ pounds through chest-high, razor-sharp elephant grass and knee-deep mud in 100-degree humidity.

Serving as the personal security detachment commander for the 4th Infantry Division's 4th Brigade Combat Team, Captain Florent “Flo” Groberg was scanning the perimeter when he noticed an individual acting suspiciously on the left side of the street, walking backward toward the patrol formation.

As the man pivoted, Groberg spotted a suicide bomb vest concealed under the man’s cloak, complete with protruding trigger wires.

With less than two seconds to react, Captain Groberg made an instantaneous decision that saved dozens of lives:

Charging the Threat: Groberg yelled a warning, abandoned cover, and charged straight at the bomber, physically shoving him backward away from the command group.

Tackling Him to the Ground: Teaming up with Sergeant Andrew Mahoney, Groberg drove the bomber into the dirt, pinning the vest against the ground with his bare hands to absorb the blast.

Disrupting the Attack: The vest detonated against the earth. The downward blast blew Groberg 20 feet into a culvert, severing 50% of his calf muscle, shattering his fibula, and causing severe burns, but preventing the primary fragmentation wave from tearing through the command group.

Triggering the Second Bomber: The shockwave caused a second concealed suicide bomber nearby to detonate prematurely into an exterior wall before he could reach the patrol.

Four American heroes were killed in the ambush—Command Sgt. Maj. Kevin J. Griffin, Maj. Thomas E. Kennedy, Air Force Maj. Walter D. Gray, and foreign service officer Ragaei Abdelfattah—but dozens more survived because Captain Groberg physically threw his body onto the threat.

On November 12, 2015, President Barack Obama presented Captain Florent Groberg with the Medal of Honor at the White House.

“HE HAD A FRACTION OF A SECOND TO SAVE HIS MEN. HE CHOSE TO SACRIFICE HIMSELF.” — The Courage of Marine Corporal Jason Dunham.

On April 14, 2004, near the Syrian border in Husaybah, Iraq, 22-year-old Marine Corporal Jason Dunham was leading a rifle squad with 3rd Battalion, 7th Marines (3/7), moving to relieve a battalion commander’s convoy that had been ambushed.

After intercepting a line of suspicious vehicles attempting to flee the area, Dunham moved in on foot to conduct a search:

 As Dunham approached, an insurgent leaped from one of the vehicles and attacked him. Dunham immediately engaged the fighter in violent hand-to-hand combat to subdue him.

During the wrestling match on the dirt road, the insurgent pulled the pin on a hand grenade and dropped it between them.

Spotting two of his Marines—Lance Corporal William Hampton and PFC Kelly Miller—rushing in to assist him, Dunham shouted a warning: “No, no, watch out!” Without hesitation, he unstrapped his Kevlar helmet, slammed it over the grenade, and threw his entire body on top, pressing down with both hands to smother the blast.

The grenade exploded, shredding the helmet and mortally wounding Dunham. But his body and helmet absorbed the overwhelming force of the blast, saving both of his fellow Marines from fatal shrapnel.

Corporal Dunham was evacuated and succumbed to his wounds eight days later on April 22, 2004, at Bethesda Naval Hospital with his parents at his bedside.

On January 11, 2007, President George W. Bush presented the Medal of Honor posthumously to his family, making Jason Dunham the first Marine in the Iraq War to receive the nation’s highest military decoration. His legacy lives on across the fleet aboard the guided-missile destroyer USS Jason Dunham (DDG-109).

In an era where so few bear the burden of service, what does Corporal Jason Dunham’s split-second decision to smother a live grenade tell us about the heart of an American Marine?

“23 POUNDS OF STEEL. HUNDREDS OF ROUNDS OF 7.62. WELCOME TO THE JUNGLE.” — The Brutal Reality of Humping “The Pig” in Vietnam.

In the dense, suffocating heat of the Vietnamese jungle, infantrymen gave the M60 machine gun a nickname that stuck for generations: “The Pig.”

It earned the name honestly—because of its bulky, cumbersome weight, ferocious appetite for belted ammunition, and bone-jarring recoil when ripping through the brush:

• The Physical Punishment: At 23.15 pounds unloaded, the M60 was already a beast to carry. Factor in a spare barrel, an asbestos heat mitt, cleaning kit, and 500 to 1,000 rounds of linked 7.62×51mm NATO ammunition draped in crisscrossed bandoliers across the gunner and assistant gunner's chests, and a gun team was humping 70+ pounds through chest-high, razor-sharp elephant grass and knee-deep mud in 100-degree humidity.

• The Squad’s Lifeline: Firing at a sustained 550 to 650 rounds per minute with an effective range of over 1,100 meters, the M60 was the squad's primary base of fire. When an infantry patrol walked into an L-shaped ambush in the triple canopy, the distinctive heavy thumping roar of "The Pig" chewing through tree trunks was the only thing that bought troops time to maneuver.

• The Quirks: Early models lacked a carrying handle on the barrel, forcing gunners to use a bulky asbestos mitt to swap out glowing-red barrels mid-firefight. It was prone to jamming in red clay dust and mud, but when properly cleaned and fed, it delivered unmatched stopping power.

To the veterans who carried or fought alongside "The Pig" in Vietnam, the Gulf, or beyond: did you love it for its devastating firepower, or curse it every time you had to hump it up a ridgeline?

“PARATROOPERS DON’T CLOCK OUT: HEARD GUNSHOTS & RAN DOWNSTAIRS WITH IMPROVISED MEDICAL GEAR.”

Paratroopers don't clock out. When gunfire erupted outside his apartment building, Sergeant Brian Lieberman didn't lock his door and wait for the police. He ran straight into the courtyard, found a victim with an open chest wound, and built an airtight chest seal with plastic wrap and tape to keep her lungs from collapsing.

On June 5, 2023, then-Specialist Brian R. Lieberman—a combat medic with the 1st Brigade Combat Team, 82nd Airborne Division—was off-duty at his apartment complex in Fayetteville, North Carolina, when rapid gunfire shattered the evening quiet.

Without body armor or advanced medical equipment, he grabbed his legally owned firearm and sprinted downstairs toward the active shooter:

Sprinting to the Fire: Arriving in the courtyard, Lieberman identified himself as an Army combat medic and located a female victim suffering from a critical penetrating sucking chest wound.

Shielding Under Secondary Fire: As he began treating her, the active shooter circled back in a vehicle and opened fire directly at them. Lieberman threw his body across the wounded woman to act as a human shield, drew his sidearm, returned fire, and drove the shooter away.

The Improvised Chest Seal: With air and blood entering her chest cavity and no standard trauma kit on hand, Lieberman improvised an occlusive chest seal using a plastic bag and tape, venting trapped air to prevent a fatal tension pneumothorax.

Fighting Traumatic Shock: He treated the victim for hypovolemic shock and kept her conscious until Fayetteville Police and EMS arrived, saving her life.

For his valor and composure, Colonel Jason Schuerger presented Sergeant Lieberman with the Soldier's Medal—the U.S. Army's highest non-combat award for heroism. In October 2026, he was formally recognized as an Angel of the Battlefield recipient.

“Without a doubt our Airborne medics move to the sound of gunfire to save lives,” said Col. Schuerger. “Of course he moved to the sound of gunfire, of course he administered aid, of course he saved somebody's life.”

Lieberman’s guidance to fellow medics reflects the heart of the Airborne:

“I always tell my junior medics to never lose their passion for the craft of medicine. That way no matter where they are, no matter what they're doing, they can always be there for someone on their worst day.”

All American valor in action.

The U.S. military has always been fertile soil for firsts throughout our nation’s history, and the promotion of Carol A. Mutter to become the nation’s first female lieutenant general serves as a perfect case in point for Women’s History Month.

Women have served in the military from the earliest years of our representative republic.

Deborah Sampson (Gannett) served covertly when she disguised herself as a man under the assumed name of Robert Shurtleff, to join the Continental Army and fight in the Revolutionary War in 1782. Sampson went so far as to cut a musket ball out of her own thigh to prevent a battlefield surgeon from discovering her true gender. She was honorably discharged as a private in 1793.

Women gained the opportunity to serve openly in World War 1 when Congress opened the military to women in 1914. However, it took more than two centuries between the time Sampson first shouldered a musket to the time when women served as general (flag rank) officers in the American military. Mutter achieved one-star brigadier general rank in 1991.

Three years later Mutter became the first woman in the history of America’s military to achieve two-star major general rank in 1994, and two years after that in 1996 she became the first woman to become a three-star lieutenant general in any American military branch.

Born in 1945 in Greeley, Colorado, Mutter graduated in 1967 from officer candidate school at the University of Northern Colorado as a second lieutenant in the Marine Corps.

Mutter had a number of firsts during her 32-year career in the Corps:

•First woman to qualify as Command Center Crew Commander/Space Director at U.S. Space Command.
• First woman of flag rank (general officer rank) to command a major deployable tactical command.
• First woman Marine major general, and senior woman in all the services at that time.
• First woman nominated by a U.S. president (Bill Clinton) for three-star rank.
• First female lieutenant general in the U.S. Armed Forces.

During a 2014 interview for the documentary Unsung Heroes: The Story of America's Female Patriots, Mutter explains why she joined the Marine Corps during the early years of the Vietnam War.

“Because they're the best, there's no doubt about that,” she said. “ ... when I joined, (the Corps) was only one percent female and there were no women in the deployed forces at all. So, as long as the women were back in the rear doing the jobs that the men didn't want to do, there was not much of a problem.”

The general has been recognized as a trailblazer by several different organizations. Among them is the National Women’s Hall of Fame, which inducted the general in 2017.

Mutter retired from the Corps in 1999 and lives with her husband at their home in Lookout Mountain, Tennessee.

Then he went back.
And back again.
And again. Six of his soldiers. While he was burning. He refused to be evacuated until every one of them was out first. He died three weeks later from the burns covering most of his body.
